niche.title: How a Cut Heals 😮
niche.description:
When you cut yourself, tiny blood vessels in your skin break open. Platelets plug the broken ends, fibrin threads trap red cells into a clot, and the clot's top dries into a scab. White blood cells squeeze out of nearby vessels to eat germs that got in. New tissue fills the gap from below, skin cells slide in under the scab, and when the scab falls off, the new tissue stays as a scar.

This is an animation, not microscopy: the cells are drawn far bigger than life, days and weeks are sped up into seconds, and in a real wound these steps overlap. Many scars fade over months.

Sources: MedlinePlu

niche.title: Broken Bones Heal Without a Scar, Unlike Most Tissues #science #howthebodyworks #anatomy
niche.description:
A twisting ski fall snaps a shin bone, and we dive inside to watch it rebuild: a blood clot bridges the gap, soft cartilage steadies the break, then it hardens into new bone. Over the following months the extra lump is carved away until the bone is back to its old shape.

Bone is one of the few tissues that heals without a scar: after months of remodelling, the break often leaves no outside trace and the bone is often just as strong as before.

Sources:
- Marsell R, Einhorn TA (2011). The biology of fracture healing. Injury 42(6):551-555 (PMC) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3105171/

​Esophagus: Peristalsis (muscular waves) pushes food smoothly down toward the stomach.
  
​Stomach: Acid and digestive enzymes mix with food to create a semi-liquid mixture called chyme.
  
​Small Intestine & Villi: Nutrients are further broken down and absorbed into the blood through tiny villi.

outliers.title: How a Cut Heals 😮
outliers.description:
When you cut yourself, tiny blood vessels in your skin break open. Platelets plug the broken ends, fibrin threads trap red cells into a clot, and the clot's top dries into a scab. White blood cells squeeze out of nearby vessels to eat germs that got in. New tissue fills the gap from below, skin cells slide in under the scab, and when the scab falls off, the new tissue stays as a scar.

This is an animation, not microscopy: the cells are drawn far bigger than life, days and weeks are sped up into seconds, and in a real wound these steps overlap. Many scars fade over months.

Sources: MedlinePlu

outliers.title: Why Hitting Your Funny Bone Hurts So Much 😖
outliers.description:
Your funny bone isn't a bone at all. It's the ulnar nerve, which runs from your neck down to your pinky and sits right under the skin at your elbow, with nothing to protect it. Bang it and you crush the nerve against bone, so the zap shoots into your ring and pinky fingers. And the name? It sits next to the humerus. 😖

Animated explainers about the weird ways the world (and your body) works. New Shorts every day.

For education and entertainment only, not medical advice.

outliers.description:
Meet Humphrey (the end of Ben's upper arm bone, sure he is broken) and Ully (the nerve who actually got hit).

The ulnar nerve gives feeling to the little finger and half of the ring finger. That is why the jolt shoots down the forearm into those two fingers although nothing touched them.

outliers.title: How Many Holes Does Your Body Have?
outliers.description:
How many holes does your body have: nine, one or zero? Topology has an answer, and it's the sequel to the straw.

Count: mouth, anus, 2 nostrils and 4 tear drains (lacrimal puncta) are 8 openings joined in one system. 8 openings - 1 = 7 through-holes. Ears are sealed by the eardrum; the other openings are dead ends. Each pierced earlobe adds one.
